speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRIBUTES AND FELICITATIONS ON HIS EIGHTIETH BIRTHDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the business of the day, and on a matter of general privilege, I feel it would be appropriate to recognize the fact that today is not only the birthday of Queen Victoria, but it is also the birthday of the senior statesman of the British fellowship throughout the world. Today in South Africa Field Marshal Smuts is celebrating his eightieth birthday. It is appropriate that here in Canada we should indicate our own good wishes to a man who has contributed so much to the development of this great British association to which we belong; to a man who in his own life has given a remarkable demonstration of the way in which friendship may grow out of understanding, and, because of the genius of our system, those who have even been enemies can stand side by side in the great cause of freedom.
Field Marshal Smuts was actually in command of the Boer troops during a considerable period of the South African war. Shortly after that, when South Africa became associated with the rest of us in this common endeavour which is called the British empire, the British commonwealth, or by whatever other term one chooses to describe this really remarkable fellowship of free people, he showed the way in which the hand of friendship can be extended after hostilities have ceased. Surely there can be nothing more dramatic than the fact that one of the most gallant soldiers on the other side of the Boer war became the commander of the South African troops in the war of 1914-18, and again during the second world war was not only prime minister of South Africa but also the supreme commander of the South African troops.
Field Marshal Smuts has been a truly remarkable man, and his service has not by any means been confined to South Africa. Today, when thoughtful people everywhere are reaching out for a wider basis of understanding among the nations of the world, it 55946-177*	*	|
is interesting to recall that, out of his early experience, he has always sought the widest measure of understanding among nations. He is the only man in public life today who was an active representative of a government at the time the charter of the league of nations came into existence at Versailles in 1919. In the spring of 1945 he went to San Francisco with the experience of a man who had seen the dream of the league of nations emerge, and had seen that dream shattered. It was he who was largely responsible for the drafting of the opening paragraphs of the declaration of the United Nations. In that declaration he sought to overcome the weaknesses of the covenant of the league, which had failed to preserve peace.
Today this man, with eighty years behind him, still shows that out of all that experience he is building for the future. I feel sure that we in this House of Commons today, far separated in distance from South Africa, would wish to extend our best wishes for many happy returns to* this great citizen of the free fellowship to which we belong.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: TRIBUTES AND FELICITATIONS ON HIS EIGHTIETH BIRTHDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is not here on this occasion, because I am sure he would have considered it a privilege to agree with what has been said by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). Indeed, he probably would have taken it upon himself to express the congratulations which have been so well expressed by the leader of the opposition.
Since the Prime Minister is not here, however, I find myself in the position of speaking for the group who sit on this side of the house, and on the other side, nearest to you, Mr. Speaker, as well; and in doing so I want to join with the leader of the opposition in the expression of the points of view he has just stated. During the Boer war, General Smuts was one of the leaders who at that time opposed us, and after the war ended in peace he took a leading part in bringing together the peoples of the southern part of the African continent, in very much the same manner as the leaders on this continent had on a previous occasion brought together the two great races here. I have no doubt that had men such as Montcalm lived through the battles of those days and
2798	HOUSE OF
Felicitations to Field Marshal Smuts settled in this country, to carry on in relation to what has happened since they would have taken much the same position as General Smuts has taken in South Africa.
I would remind hon. members that when the terms of peace were being discussed and new organizations were being set up in South Africa to meet the new situation, Canada was copied perhaps to a greater extent than any other part of the British commonwealth. From that time until this, General Smuts has taken a great interest in what has been going on in this country, and in doing so has tended to bring our peoples closer and closer together. By applying the same practices and principles in the southern part of Africa as were followed here, he has done much in many parts of world to promote the interests of the commonwealth as they have been promoted here.
For these reasons it gives me great pleasure to join the leader of the opposition in extending congratulations to this grand old man who in his own country has seen so many of his efforts brought to fruition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said he was speaking for the group with which he is associated, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said he was speaking for the party sitting on the government side, which has an overflow on this side, they really expressed the sentiment of all hon. members, no matter where they may sit in the house.
I have much pleasure in associating the members of the C.C.F. party with the felicitations extended to Field Marshal Smuts. I believe the story of the lives of Smuts and Botha, and some of their associates who were leaders of the Boer forces against the armies of the empire during the Boer war, indicates that they rendered notable service in promoting the welfare of this commonwealth of nations.
Our good wishes go out to Field Marshal Smuts today, particularly in view of the disturbed conditions that prevail in South Africa. The field marshal has taken a much more moderate attitude than some others do toward racial difficulties in that country; and I hope the day is not far distant when the people of South Africa will join with the other members of the commonwealth in banishing for ever the racial discrimination that now mars the good name of the Union of South Africa.

speakeroldname: Hon. Siuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PERSONS LISTED IN NOTEBOOK OF KLAUS FUCHS
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) asked me a question in the following terms:
Has there been any examination or re-examination of the loyalty of any of the 150 persons then resident in Canada listed in the notebook found as a result of the espionage investigations of 1945 and 1946, since the trial ot Dr. Fuchs?
The notebook referred to in the hon. member's question was in fact a pocket address book, containing, as the question indicates, the names of 150 persons then resident in Canada. It formed only one item of many thousands of documents seized in the searches made in conjunction with the arrests of spy suspects in 1946. In this mass of material so seized there were many such notebooks; also desk calendars, memo pads, telephone finders, mailing lists, etc., which

contained thousands of names, addresses, telephone numbers and miscellaneous entries. All this material was carefully examined, including the notebook in question.
The list of 150 names referred to was carefully checked to ascertain which of these 150 names, if any, were those of persons who could be suspected of espionage or subversive activity. It was found that a limited number of the persons named belonged to either or both of these groups. In all such cases where positive identification proved possible, the entries were then related to and dealt with on the appropriate investigation files. As some of these investigations are still current, it will be appreciated that it would not be desirable to specify the number of persons identified.
The majority of the entries in this notebook, however, refer to professional people and others of good repute whose loyalty is beyond question.
All these investigation files have since remained extant. They, and the notebook in question, have been examined from time to time as a matter of security routine on every occasion, both before and after the trial of Dr. Fuchs, when information secured in other police investigations or from other sources indicated that such re-examination might contribute to and strengthen security measures.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not time to give continuity to the remarks I was making last night by recapitulating what I said. My concluding words were that we had not yet received word from any senior government as to what financial aid was to be given. I shall deal with the provincial government later. At the moment let me deal with the federal government.
We have been told that aid will be given on the same terms as aid was given to those who suffered from the floods in the Fraser valley. I feel that that would be excellent, if it is correct. I am informed that a grant of $5 million was given to British Columbia in the case of the Fraser valley, which rather more than covered rehabilitation costs. An order in council, P.C. 2644, passed in June, 1948, declared the British Columbia flood to be "a national disaster so serious and pressing

Manitoba Flood
as to make it necessary for the good government of Canada that the government of Canada join with the government of British Columbia in taking relief and rehabilitation measures."
I know of no such statement being made so far about the flood situation in Manitoba. I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has called it a misfortune of the first order, whereas we in Manitoba are inclined to call it, on the basis of our experience, a national disaster. When the Prime Minister was in Winnipeg the other day he attended this by now notorious press conference. He was asked by a reporter if the government had formally recognized the flood as a national emergency. As reported in the Winnipeg Free Press for May 22, 1950, he replied:
I do not like the words "national emergency." When something happens to Canadians, then all Canadians are interested. Already there is ample proof of the widespread effect upon Canadians that this flood has had.
May I say that there is most widespread and generous proof indeed, but not yet proof from the senior governments. At a later stage the Prime Minister was asked if he had found the picture as black as it had been painted, and he replied, "Perhaps not". We are told on the front page of the Winnipeg Free Press that the Prime Minister made a four-hour tour of the dikes. One cannot hope to see the misery which prevails in the community in a tour lasting only four hours. The Prime Minister also said at the same conference that relatives of his had been affected by floods, that they had recovered and re-established themselves by their own efforts, and so far as they were concerned good luck to them. But the Prime Minister's relatives did not have the flood problems from which the people of Point Douglas in Winnipeg are suffering today. Working class people there have lost their homes and their jobs. Families have been evacuated to points all over the prairies.
In British Columbia the grant was for one phase of the flood. We do not know whether that is going to be so in Manitoba. In addition to the grant there was, however, another seventy-five per cent paid by the federal government toward the cost of fighting the floods, and for the building of permanent dikes. I should also like to point out that the commission which has been appointed has been requested to ascertain the cost of emergency precautions to guard against the recurrence of floods. We are not at all interested in emergency precautions. What we are interested in is something much more permanent. It is plain that the federal government must make its position amply clear so that the people of Winnipeg and Manitoba generally may know where they stand.

I think it only right that I should indicate in chronological order the sequence of events. Here I want to refer to the Winnipeg Tribune, a newspaper to which C have made uncomplimentary references in the past and to which I shall probably refer in the same way in future. I am retracting those references for the period of this crisis, however, for this newspaper has shown courage, vision and a consciousness of responsibility which I find heart-warming in a time such as this. On April 4 the newspaper reported that there were serious floods along the Red river in North Dakota. I believe the permanent officials of the provincial government knew of the situation long before that and that they advised their superiors; nevertheless no action was taken. On April 10 this newspaper warned the people that snow and cold would increase the city flood danger. No action was taken by the premier. On April 11 the Tribune warned the city that floods threatened its well-being; still no action by the premier. On April 12 the people of Fort Garry and East Kildonan, without any help, started to reinforce their own dikes; still no word from the premier. On April 14 an agreement was entered into with the Department of National Defence under which the province of Manitoba agreed to pay for whatever services were rendered; yet the services of the army, the navy and the air force were not utilized until May 6.
I can find no explanation for such a lack of action. It may have been a complete failure to appreciate the devastation which threatened. It may have been a matter of pettifogging parsimony; I do not know. I am only reciting facts as I know them.
On April 18 the Red Cross proclaimed that the floods at Grand Forks in the United States were a disaster; no word from the premier. On April 21 the river was over its banks in certain areas of Winnipeg; the premier was quiet. On April 24 the river was two feet under the 1948 peak; still no word from the premier of Manitoba. On the same date Elm Park, a residential area, was cut off; yet the premier was silent. On May 1, as hon. members will recall, members of all parties in this house discussed the matter of the floods in Manitoba, and we urged the premier of that province to declare it a national emergency. Still he was silent. During that week thousands of homes were evacuated; still there was silence. Thousands of people left the city; the silence continued.
Finally, on May 6, Brigadier Morton, G.O.C. prairie command, was appointed controller of flood relief; but let there be no misunderstanding as to the meaning of that word

"controller". It meant very little indeed; ior when I went to the dikes and asked people who was in charge, they said no one was in charge. They were doing the work themselves, without supervision or direction, in order that they might save the city. The army had no power either to requisition materials that were needed or to direct people to the areas which needed help most. During those days the Winnipeg Free Press was asking for some centralized control or authority that could give priority to the needs of the city, but to the best of my knowledge that action was never taken.
When I speak of Brigadier Morton, let me take this opportunity to pay tribute to the tremendous efforts of the men of the navy, the army and the R.C.A.F. to help save the city. In particular, my colleagues here from Quebec might be interested to learn that the men of the Vingt-deux regiment played a great part in building that forty-foot dike which today protects the city hydro power station from immersion.
Finally, on May 7, the premier of Manitoba asked the federal government to recognize the situation in that province as a national disaster. Only then did he make his request, but after that he resumed the lethargy which had characterized him up to that time and said nothing more, even though representatives of the city and municipalities went to him and pleaded for some statement as to what part of the cost the province would be prepared to bear. Still there was silence. A meeting of that kind took place only a week ago, and the only result was a wire from the premier to the Prime Minister of Canada asking him to visit the flood area. The premier would give no commitment to those people who were carrying on the battle against the flood. By his silence he piled indecision upon frustration. It is true that night after night he would go on the air to tell the people what he thought was happening. He told of the grand work the people themselves were doing, and of the committees that were going to be set up to help them, but there was not a definite word as to what assistance would be forthcoming to any municipality. Then, just about a week ago today, he told us that his conscience was clear. No one had questioned the clarity of his conscience. No one gave a continental red cent as to the condition of his conscience. A statement like that shows how fatuity has been heaped upon futility by the provincial government throughout.
Today the people are still doing the job that has to be done. Our citizens, without leadership, have shown that inner strength
Manitoba Flood
which comes to free people in times like these. They went out and provided their own leadership to do the job that had to be done.
My words of criticism of the leadership in the province should not in any way lead hon. members to think that the need for help is not great indeed. There are those who have travelled with tragedy; who, as far as practical offers of help are concerned, are still doomed to dwell in despair. What is the reaction of the premier to this?; Just a few days ago he broke his silence and said that, in cases of need, substantial financial help would be forthcoming. What he meant was that there would be a means test on misery; and that is precisely what is happening. Families have lost everything. There is a tension amongst those who know they have nothing left in the world. There is a tension amongst those who fear they may still lose everything they have; yet we have no leadership and no hope of leadership from the provincial government.
Now, what are the needs? Over 100,000 people have been evacuated. I hope many of them may be able to return to their homes very shortly. Many others will not be able to go back to their homes for several months. Here, then, is a terrific problem in social rehabilitation. How are those people to be kept away from Winnipeg? Who is going to pay the cost if they have to board in other areas or other cities? The Prime Minister says some 8,000 homes have been damaged. I do not think that is correct; I dispute it. The figure is over 12,000 or I miss my guess. Not only have homes been irretrievably damaged; whole city streets have gone. I know of one stretch in my own constituency, at Cathedral and Aikens, which has collapsed to a depth of four feet. Today the city is literally resting on water.
What is the condition of the homes? Take the place in which I used to live, for instance, where the water is right up to the ceiling. Obviously the plaster will be destroyed; and this applies to all homes of that kind. If there is stucco on the outside it will be ruined. If there is insulation it will have soaked up water right to the top storey. All that insulation will have to be torn out; and anyone who knows anything about houses will realize what a task that is. Flooring is completely sprung. Joists, sills and beams are swollen and twisted out of shape, because this water has not been there for only a few days; in many cases it has been there for three weeks, and may well be there for another three weeks. Electrical appliances and electrical wiring are ruined. All these things will have to be rebuilt. In effect new

Manitoba Flood
houses will have to be built; and that will perhaps give members an indication of the task which faces us.
I maintain that the very least we can do in the face of this disaster, a disaster which perhaps the insurance companies may term an act of God, is that there should be complete rehabilitation for the victims of these floods. I doubt very much whether the generosity of either this government or the provincial government will permit that to be done, because the damage is extraordinary. I would hesitate to hazard a guess, but if I say the damage amounts to $100 million I am sure I shall not be far out. If we are not going to have complete rehabilitation, then I suggest as the very minimum that all those who receive salaries up to $300 a month be put back in their homes as they were before the flood and without cost to them; all those who receive salaries between $300 and $400 a month might perhaps get ninety per cent, and all those between $400 and $500 a month might perhaps receive eighty per cent. All this, of course, would be subject to any payments made by insurance companies.
I suggest further that those who have lost money due to the floods be permitted to charge those losses against income tax next year. There is a commission to assess the damages which has been asked to give this house accurate data. It will not be possible for any commission to give this house accurate data in time for us to consider the report before the house rises. The best it can do is to give us a progress report, but even then the commission will have to be arbitrary. How will it assess the damages? Will it go around to each house, in each locality, and say that so much damage has been suffered? How can the commission state the damage when the damage will not be seen for months yet? There is only one thing which can be done, and that is to make the houses livable, to refurnish them as far as possible so that the owners may live in them. After that, we can find out the cost.
Let me say that the construction industry and the electrical industry in Winnipeg are more than willing to co-operate with civic authorities. They have already indicated they are at the disposal of the municipality in the tremendous task of rebuilding homes. The electrical industry, for instance, has said that a meeting would be held to decide what charges should be made for each particular item of repair. Flat rates would be set up, and there would be no profiteering by that industry. The building industry has to be mobilized, but what about the contractor who has contracts to build other houses? I do not

think this is the time for building new houses. There is too great a problem of rehabilitation, and in some way or other the contractors will have to be protected against suits for breach of contract if they do emergency work. There will be a great demand for skilled craftsmen, such as carpenters, electricians and plasterers. The Department of Labour must,consider this problem. There are not enough craftsmen of these types in Manitoba, so we may need a reserve of skilled labour upon which we can draw.
Those are just some of the problems which face us. I could continue enumerating them almost indefinitely, as I am sure other members could, but time does not permit. There is a job of work to be done. I can assure members that every contribution they make to the fund which is being raised in the house is going to be needed desperately. Every contribution which the people of Canada can make is going to be equally needed. It is not right that the people themselves should have to suffer because of the indecision of their leaders. In the final analysis, the collective responsibility of our society, and the financial power of our society, lies in the parliament of Canada. Our people are stricken. As I said before they are not out, and they never will be out; but they are grievously hurt. The federal government must be more positive than it has been up to the present. It must be more generous than it has yet indicated it intends to be.
May I suggest that at the moment the most practical thing we could do here would be to establish a minimum grant in aid, an interim payment as it were, of about $10 million, which could be given to the provincial government, so that it, in turn, could hand the money over to the municipalities to enable them to assume the responsibility which the provincial government has given up by default.

Mr. Speaker, as has been pointed out by the previous speaker (Mr. Stewart) the Winnipeg Tribune of April 4 carried headlines to the effect that the Red river floods in North Dakota were becoming alarming. Everyone knows that the Red river flows north through Manitoba from North Dakota. It is quite some time since April 4, and I am told by very reliable authorities that the engineers in the United States, from both North Dakota and Minnesota, have shown fine co-operation with the authorities of Manitoba. I believe that to be true.
I wish to refer to a statement by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) which is to be found on page 2478 of Hansard of

May 15. I am not finding fault with the statement, but I want to clarify it to some extent. It reads as follows:
Right from May 6, the day on which Premier Campbell as head of the provincial authorities instructed Brigadier General Morton to take over, he and his staff have been performing a simply magnificent feat of organization and direction.
With that I agree. Now, to people of military service at least, that statement instructing Brigadier General Morton to take over should be clarified. He has only been given authority to fight the flood and to say what districts should be evacuated. That is as far as his authority extends. Then the Red Cross takes over, and it is in charge of the evacuation of the people. I want to say that organization has done a magnificent job. Brigadier Morton and his staff of some 4,000 service personnel and 50,000 civilian volunteers have done a splendid job, as has the Red Cross, the railway companies and their employees, the bus companies and their employees, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Many other organizations have taken part.
I want to make that clear, because many people in Manitoba think that the military had complete authority from that date forward, and that is not so. In fact I shall give the house a concrete example. In Premier Campbell's own constituency there are two airports, one just outside Portage la Prairie, and one at Macdonald. The buildings at these airports I believe could accommodate a thousand people each, but no one had authority to use those buildings. I wanted to make that quite clear. It was referred to in the Winnipeg Free Press of May 12. The editorial reads as follows:
Many people assume that Brigadier Morton, in the present situation, is the agent of the federal government and in charge of the fight against the flood. He is not either one or the other. He is the agent of the province which is paying the cost of the services of the military employed in the flood. Able and resourceful as he is showing himself to be, he has been given no power. He has no powers except over a limited number of military personnel and such results as he can secure by persuasion. The statements regarding the national emergency, made last Saturday and Monday, do not alter in any respect the responsibility of the provincial government.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend permit me to clarify the matter to which he has referred? Representations were made to me with respect to making the airports around Portage la Prairie available, and I immediately took up the matter with the proper authorities. Incidentally, the ownership of the buildings is an involved matter, but I was finally assured by the Minister of National Defence, that the problem was within the control of
Manitoba Flood
the army officers in Winnipeg and the buildings would be available for use at their discretion if requested.

I thank the hon. member for that information, but as I have already pointed out, the army authorities have no authority beyond fighting the flood itself and stating what districts should be evacuated. The authority of the armed forces terminated at that point; therefore the responsibility was that of the Manitoba provincial government.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: In that same connection I might say that the army authorities did go to inspect these buildings to which my hon. friend has referred in case they might be needed for greater service in evacuating people. The inspection was made and the whole set-up reviewed as one being available if required.

The parliamentary
assistant to the Minister of Finance made a rather significant statement this afternoon on the orders of the day when he said that the Fraser river valley commission was appointed not so much to obtain information as to do a job, which they did. That seems to be the real difference between the handling of the Fraser river situation in 1948 and the Red river flood of today. There is a real difference. I pointed that out to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) yesterday when I asked him whether he had any idea as to when this commission might report. I also pointed out to him how difficult it might be for him to answer the question. Apparently this commission can get information only and report back, as I understand it. I may be wrong.	,
I asked further whether there had been a request from the Manitoba government for an interim grant, as was done for the British Columbia government in the Fraser river flood in 1948, and the Prime Minister said, not to his knowledge. I am surprised there has not been a request of that kind from the provincial government.
If one has not seen the situation out there, as has the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), the Prime Minister, and I think all the members from Manitoba, one cannot appreciate it. I was there on the first day of the evacuation to any great extent. On the night before I was there and on that day they moved out over 15,000 people. I talked with railway people who had not slept for forty-eight hours. Unless you saw these mothers and little children gathered around them with no means left, you cannot appreciate it. I went through one of the special trains and I interviewed many people who had not a dollar of

Manitoba Flood
their own money with them. The Red Cross had looked after the transportation, but they were not sure where they were going.
Apart from shells bursting over a city, I have never seen anything that looked more like the picture I witnessed during the first war in France and Belgium when the evacuation from the front lines area was taking place. That is how it impressed me at that time. These people have gone through a great deal. Since then-I am not sure of the figures-in the neighbourhood of 100,000 people have been evacuated from Winnipeg. The people, who out of the generosity of their hearts have taken these families into their homes, and the municipal corporations, are responsible for them.
Yesterday I received a letter from the mayor of a town in my constituency which is at the far end of the province from Winnipeg. They are happy to be looking after these people, and he told me of their problems. He said that the town corporation and the rural municipalities are financing the entire business without, so far, a promise of reimbursement from anybody. He was not complaining about it. He was writing about some other matters, and happened to point out the situation.
As a citizen of Manitoba I am very sorry to say that the only organization that has failed, and has failed miserably to date, has been our provincial government and our Premier Campbell. I do not think people can misconstrue my making that statement, because I have been a supporter of the coalition government. I voted for one of their candidates last fall. I am ashamed of the situation today. I have been in and out of Winnipeg several times in the past few days and have seen this matter from several angles, and what I say is my candid opinion. I want to say in all fairness that some departments of the government and many government employees have done and are doing a magnificent job with respect to the disastrous Manitoba Red river flood problem. I think I should say that on behalf of these people.
The department of public works?

I am not mentioning any names. I want to say that they too did a good job. I did not see the minister of public works when I was in Winnipeg, but I have seen his staff. I can tell you that on one Sunday the entire staff worked from daylight to dark.
I do not know where the minister was. I presume he was busy in cabinet council. As I say, I did not see him. The deputy minister of public works and his staff worked from 
daylight to dark and did a magnificent job,, as did other members of the provincial government. I saw that myself.
I want to say something about the statement of Mayor Garnet Coulter*, whom I have known for many years. In fact when I had the honour of being president of the Manitoba union of municipalities he was then an aider-man in the city of Winnipeg and a member of the executive serving with me. I always considered him a mild-mannered, even-tempered, careful public official, careful about his statements. I think anybody else who has known him will bear me out in that statement. When I read in the newspapers that he was reported as saying-and as I listened to the report over the air-that Premier Campbell was guilty of criminal negligence, I was surprised. I was surprised at that language coming from him, but that is how serious the matter has become.
Many of us from Manitoba used to know Mrs. McQueen and her husband, who was killed in an air crash going west doing war service work. Mrs. McQueen is now doing social service work in Manitoba. According to the press, she used the very same terms. This is a serious business. Both of these public officials stated that Premier Campbell and his government were guilty of causing undue mental suffering to many of these people. As I say, I am sorry about that whole situation.
I said something about the municipalities taking care of these people. On the radio farmers for forty or fifty miles around Winnipeg who had farm tractors that were useful, large trucks and all that kind of thing, were appealed to. They were asked to come in and use that equipment in Winnipeg. I witnessed some of these huge trucks getting into difficulties in the subway going across to St. Boniface. You have all heard and read much of the Norwood dike. I want to tell you of the great piece of human effort that was put into that dike. It has been nothing short of a miracle that it has stood up and that there has been no great loss of life. But I watched those huge trucks going into the subway in several feet of water. The motors would stall, and a caterpillar tractor would be hitched onto them in an endeavour to pull them out and the chain would snap. Any man who is familiar with machinery or is of a mechanical turn of mind knows what damage that would do to those motors and to that equipment. These farmers have been doing that kind of work, supplying their own gas and fuel and that type of equipment without any promise of satisfactory reimbursement. In fact those from Manitoba will bear this in mind. The [DOT]See also page 2850.

city of St. Boniface has gone through financial difficulties, and they are not yet in a position to make expenditures of that kind freely. They are making a great comeback; it is a great city, but they are in an embarrassing financial situation right now. I just give that as a concrete example of the difficulties.
There is a great deal of that kind of work being done by private individuals, and some municipalities are not even in shape to reimburse those people who should at least have some definite promise, because it is just about two months since the first warning was given; and even the rural people, whom we are now forgetting to some extent because of the great disaster in the city of Winnipeg, were first to be overrun in this flood. Their homes were flooded, and many of them were destroyed. Some of their stock were lost and they went through terrible difficulties. That is now quite a while ago.
I do not want to repeat many of the arguments that have been made by the previous speakers. I recently received a letter from the Winnipeg chamber of commerce, dated May 15, 1950, which reads as follows:
At an emergent meeting of the executive of the Winnipeg chamber of commerce held Saturday morning, the following resolution was unanimously adopted:
The chamber Is strongly of the opinion that capital costs and/or restoration and reconstruction of damage occasioned by the flood are the sole responsibility of senior governments and that the chamber make strong representation to the authorities concerned in support of this position. Further, that funds supplied by these governments be administered by a strong independent commission appointed jointly by the senior governments.
With that resolution I agree. That is the least that can be expected.
Then, with respect to the campaign for funds for Manitoba flood relief, in my opinion that certainly deserves the wholehearted support of every citizen and every organization throughout the nation. One may hear the argument that this was advertising on the part of the T. Eaton Company. But, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) in connection with the great contributions made by people throughout this nation to the Fraser valley flood relief, I can tell you that if some people had been living in Manitoba, where I was, last year, and listened to some ministers of this government stating that you could not trust a past head of an Ontario government, and other eastern people, then this contribution by this great company which originated in the east is very heartening.
It is heartening to know that the T. Eaton Company and other companies have done
Manitoba Flood
what they have. One thinks of the employees of the T. Eaton Company, which originated in eastern Canada, raising over $153,000, and this sum was matched dollar for dollar by the company executive, making a total of $307,000 from that organization. Surely that gives one fresh faith in humanity. That is being done not only within this nation, but in other nations throughout the world.
I hold in my hand a quotation which states:
To pity distress is but human; to relieve it is God-like.
So long ago wrote the American philosopher Horace Mann as he meditated on the spontaneous kindness of warm-hearted people of differing faiths and beliefs as they instinctively rushed to aid their fellow human beings in great distress.
The people of southern Manitoba have suffered a catastrophe from flood unequalled in the history of Canada. All those in a rural area containing twelve towns and villages, seventy miles long and thirty miles wide, have been obliged suddenly to leave their farms and homes. Everything they possessed is under water, much of their belongings and a good deal of their livestock and seed is destroyed. Tens of thousands of city people in Winnipeg likewise have had to flee from their homes, leaving behind clothing, household equipment, furniture and possessions of all kinds.
These thousands of refugees-men, women and children alike-now sit sad and bewildered in strange places, far from their once happy farms and homes, wondering what the future holds for them.
But their hearts will be gladdened, their spirits uplifted and their hopes renewed as they hear the tidings that their warm-hearted fellow citizens are donating generously to the Manitoba flood relief fund. Contributions made to this most worthy fund will relieve human distress and, more, will ennoble the giver.
I should like to refer to a question asked on the orders of the day. I did realize that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) announced that contributions of this nature would be exempt from taxation. I believe that under the act goes to the extent of five per cent for corporations and ten per cent for individuals of income. I know personally of individuals who have already obligated themselves to charitable institutions to the extent of ten per cent of their incomes. Some people did that for their churches alone.
Then, in respect of corporations, it has been pointed out by an organization in Toronto that if full exemptions were granted in respect of contributions, throughout the province of

Manitoba Flood
Ontario alone one-half the proposed fund of $10 million would be raised. They point out that they believe those corporations would raise $5 million in that province alone. Surely this should be given serious consideration. I know of individuals who, as I say, have obligated themselves to the extent of ten per cent to their churches alone. There are branches of the Legion, and many other charitable institutions to which people make donations each year. If they wish to increase those amounts, surely they should be granted exemptions above the ten per cent for individuals and the five per cent for corporations.
I do not know how to go about it, but I would like to be able to bring some pressure to bear on our provincial government, to give a greater lead for the benefit of these poor, suffering human beings in Manitoba. I have talked with people who have put all their investments into their homes in Winnipeg. In earlier statements I have referred more particularly to rural areas. But those people in Winnipeg have been paying for their homes on the instalment plan, and buying furniture in the same way, in many cases to the extent that they did not have a dollar with which to get out of the flooded area. Surely the senior governments will give these people a greater lead than they have yet seen.
I have seen some terribly disappointed people out there. And while the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is sitting here I wish to say this, that I have heard many people in Winnipeg state publicly that they think the premier of Manitoba has depended too much for advice on the ex-premier of Manitoba, now the minister from Manitoba in this government. If that is not right, then I hope the Minister of Justice will make it clear, because one may take that from his statement which can be read in Hansard for May 1.
As I say, that is the prevalent feeling among those people. Many thousands are in a troubled state of mind. I hope that as members of this House of Commons we can put pressure on the provincial government in Manitoba to give greater leadership to the people of that province who are greatly distressed as a result of this most terrible catastrophe that has befallen any part of this nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Siuari S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it certainly had not been my intention to take part in this debate. I feel sure that if the level which was set by the admirable statement by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) had been maintained, I never should have taken part in it. Let me pay my small tribute to the leader of the opposition:

there have been very few occasions where in any gathering I have heard a statement that was more appropriate to the occasion than the one he made in this same connection yesterday.
It is therefore most regrettable that the hon. member who has just taken his seat has not seen fit to follow the example of his leader.
My leader has not been out on the ground there yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would repeat my statement whether my hon. friend the leader of the opposition had been on the ground or not because, if I may be permitted to say so, I have sufficient confidence in the leader of the opposition to believe that if he had been there he would still act in the same way he did yesterday.
May I make this clear, that I speak today in this House of Commons with a strong bias. Members of the present Manitoba government, both Liberal and Conservative, were personal friends and colleagues of mine over a considerable period of years. During that time I had never associated with men of greater loyalty, better judgment or greater experience in public life than they displayed. The very Premier Campbell, whom my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Ross) now traduces, is a man who went into the legislature in 1922 and has continued to enjoy the confidence of his constituents, and whose government has continued to enjoy the confidence of the people of Manitoba during the intervening twenty-eight years. '
Speaking with that bias, and speaking in my capacity as a private member of this House of Commons-not as a member of the government-I think it is very desirable that there should be placed upon the record certain facts if for no other reason than that the position of Manitoba shall not be misrepresented in respect of the appeal for funds which is being made.
I am free to confess that, although these gentlemen are friends of mine, in one important respect they have been, in my judgment, derelict.
In this modern age when industry and government pay a good deal of attention to public relations, and for the most part have their public relations in the hands of professionals, my friends and former colleagues in Manitoba were. so busy doing a job that I regret to say they seriously neglected to tell the people of Manitoba and the world of the job they were doing. Having regard to the fact that in a disaster of this sort the maintenance of public confidence is an important element in the handling

of the situation I would be free to confess that in that regard they are subject to criticism.
In respect of that shortcoming, they provided their own penalty of being seriously misjudged by a number of sincere people, two of whom we have heard this afternoon in this debate. For in spite of the fact that I disagree with both hon. gentlemen in some matters I believe they are fair-minded and would not be disposed to criticize too severely if they were convinced there was no proper ground for doing so.
I intend to relate certain facts this afternoon, but I do not think I could achieve any greater over-all effect upon the minds of my listeners than by describing a short episode which took place when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) met the reeves and mayors and representatives of the municipalities concerned in the Fort Garry hotel in Winnipeg last Sunday night.
Because of the travel over water and land that was necessary many of the reeves in the rural areas found it impossible to be present, but there was at least one reeve from a rural area present. I had rather gained the impression from this storm of criticism which appeared in certain newspapers and on the part of certain members of the House of Commons that when this meeting with the representatives of the municipalities took place there would be more protest and criticism against both governments, in particular against the provincial government which was represented at the meeting by Premier Campbell himself.
When his turn came to report, this rural reeve said, "We have no complaint to make. We were advised six weeks ago by a representative of the provincial government in plenty of time to make all necessary preparations for the flood. Of course no kind of preparation would enable us to cope with a flood of this size. But we took every step that was possible and were as well prepared as we could be for the flood when it did come." He then went on to relate what assistance they had been receiving, and I intend to lay the statistics with regard to this assistance before the house, and indicated that they wanted to carry on on that basis.
There was none of the deep anxiety and apprehension voiced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), nor was there any of the criticism that has been voiced by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). These people were right in the middle of the flood and were responsible to the municipal citizens. -All this bears 55946-178

out a report which I placed on the record on one of the previous occasions when I addressed the house.
To what official is the minister referring?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was Reeve Arthur Beau-bien of St. Jean, whom my hon. friend knows personally and who is a very good man.
He is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course he is. This experience bears out what I told the members of this house on a previous occasion when I voiced my admiration for what the provincial government had done.
May I say to the hon. member for Souris, if he thinks I am trying to take some credit for having advised them, that I must expressly disclaim it because being a reasonably modest man I do not undertake to advise people how to cope with a disaster which is taking place 1,500 miles away when they are in the midst of it and I am on the outside.
The report I previously put on the record was made in writing by John Conner, head of the livestock branch of the department of agriculture. If I am not mistaken, the hon. member for Souris said that he is a very fine man.
He certainly is. I know him quite well.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Hon. members will perhaps recall that the first report was made on April 28 after he had returned from a trip through this area. He stated that he had gone out to warn the people that a flood was coming. Reeve Beaubien told us that the provincial authorities had warned him, had told him that the flood would be two feet higher than it was in 1948, and that the steps they would have to take to meet the situation would have to take that additional height into account. Conner's report was to the effect that many farmers, having so recently suffered the 1948 flood, had taken steps already before he warned them to evacuate their animals, their seed, their feed and the like.
It certainly does not look as though the government were lacking in foresight. It does not look as though they were, as I understood the hon. member for Souris to imply, paying no attention to the views of United States engineers. But they did not have to pay any attention to the views of United States engineers. At a critical stage of the flood they brought up a man-

I gave credit to certain departments and to certain government officials for the splendid work that was being done.

Manitoba Flood

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall deal with the departments to which my hon. friend did not give credit. By a most extraordinary coincidence the department to which he gave credit, public works, happens to be headed by a Conservative minister.
The minister has referred to Mr. Conner, who is a member of the department of agriculture in the provincial government. He is one of the finest officials in the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend and I can agree that Mr. Conner is a fine man.
I will agree with that also.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I was saying, they did not need to have the advice of United States engineers because when they brought a United States engineer up to Manitoba at the request of certain people who wanted to be reassured one statement that he made was this: "I wonder why you went to the trouble of bringing me up here from the Twin Cities when you have here in the person of Don Stephens, deputy minister of mines and resources, a man who knows more about the Red river than I." I believe the hon. member for Souris will agree with that.

I respect him as an
engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That was the basis of the information that they had; that was the basis of the action that was taken. At an early stage in the proceedings the government of Manitoba entered into an agreement. This was a long while before Brigadier Morton was put in charge; that came later. They entered into an agreement in case the flood, which it was anticipated would be two feet higher than the 1948 level, by some unforeseen circumstance rose to a still greater height, to provide that the army would in the meanwhile have some legal status and be ready to take over at a moment's notice. The prognostication of the engineers proved to be remarkably accurate. The flood rose to about that level.
I remember the circumstances very well because I was in the midst of them a little over two weeks ago when I visited Winnipeg over that week end. I am sure that those who have been back to their constituencies will bear me out that for a couple of days there were heavy rains throughout the whole of the Red river valley.
And snow.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The expert brought from the United States is authority for the statement that those rains, falling on the various tributary streams in the Red river valley, accounted for not less than an increase of

four feet in the level of the river. This created in a matter of a day, in fact in a matter of hours, an emergency of the direst character. On Friday or Saturday night-I am not sure which-after I had had a pretty strenuous day spent in part on the river in the Kingston Crescent area, I was on the point of going to bed when I received an emergency telephone call from Premier Campbell asking me to attend a meeting of all the city and municipal authorities, engineers, officials of the health department, various other civic and provincial officials, the army, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Red Cross and the like to deal with this emergency piled upon an emergency created by the heavy rainfall on top of the spring flood.
I cannot recall whether I indicated this before, but one of the first steps that had to be taken after midnight that night was to evacuate the tuberculosis and contagious diseases hospitals operated by the city of Winnipeg in the Riverview area. Because of the great rainfall that was taking place the dikes in that area were said by the engineers to be in such a condition that they could not guarantee they would hold until morning. If the leadership and the provision for the immediate future to which my hon. friend has referred was one-quarter as bad as he painted it, they might have had casualties in evacuating those hospitals. In a matter of minutes almost they had to evacuate people suffering from tuberculosis and contagious diseases, and transfer them to another hospital where provision for quarantine had to be made. If the government had not three weeks before, with the assistance and co-operation of the Red Cross, made all the necessary arrangements for the evacuation of those hospitals, it would have been impossible to carry it out that night.
To which government does the minister refer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am referring to the provincial government. It would have been impossible to accomplish this evacuation if the provincial authorities were as bad as the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) says they were. Practically out of a blue sky we were told by these highly competent engineers-
Which department would that be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The engineers?
No, the one concerned with the evacuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would be the health department.
I give high credit to the department and its minister right now, and he is a Liberal too.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am very glad to hear that. We may gradually get down to the things my hon. friend thinks were not right. It appears to me that he is searching around for a scapegoat upon whom to put all the sins of Israel.
No, I am not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We can be sure the scapegoat will not be a Conservative. To give hon. members some conception of how urgent the situation was, the meeting lasted until about half past two in the morning. At that meeting Brigadier Morton and the army were put in charge of the whole situation. When the hon. member for Souris, and to a lesser extent the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), although I am not quite sure that I understood the meaning of all he said because although I am a Scotsman myself-
You are not Scotch enough.

May I ask
on what point the minister is not clear?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There was the odd word or phrase I did not get the meaning of, and therefore I am refraining from quoting my hon. friend to any great extent.
What I said was that the army did not have effective control.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am glad to have that interjection because the position the hon. member takes is pretty much the same as that of the hon. member for Souris.
It is true, isn't it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am coming to that very point, and this is a good introduction to my remarks. I speak with a certain amount of personal knowledge because I was present and took some part in the meeting which decided to put the army in charge. The Red Cross and all these other organizations were represented there and, believe me, Mr. Speaker, we did not split any legal hairs or engage in legal technicalities as to the precise legal status of the army. Everyone present at the meeting agreed to have Brigadier Morton put in charge. They wanted to have one man to boss the show and they said, "If you come in we will do what you tell us." He said, "I am quite willing to tell you what to do but I want your advice. You advise me as to the decisions I have to make when I order you and we shall all get along splendidly together." And that is how they have got along.
